01


**TL;DR**


- Can embedded finance platforms issue cards? Yes, when an approved issuing program supports the intended use case.
- Virtual cards suit online purchasing; physical cards suit in-person spending. Confirm controls and acceptance for each program.
- Card issuance is separate from bank accounts, payment routing, and stablecoin settlement.
- Infinite serves global businesses needing multicurrency accounts and cross-border payment routing; assess card issuance separately.


02


## Why this matters


**Buying payment infrastructure is not the same as buying a card program.** A provider can move funds between accounts without supplying card credentials, handling card disputes, or supporting physical card delivery. Treat those capabilities as separate requirements.


That distinction matters when you compare[banking-as-a-service providers](https://infinite.net/learn/insights/best-banking-as-a-service-providers) . Start with the transaction your customer needs to complete, then identify the infrastructure and contractual responsibilities behind it. For a 2026 evaluation, a broad platform description is not a substitute for a documented issuing scope.


03


## Can embedded finance platforms issue physical and virtual cards?


Yes. An embedded finance platform can expose card-issuing capabilities inside another company's software, letting approved users access physical cards, virtual cards, or both. The issuing institution remains distinct from the software interface unless the platform itself holds the relevant issuing authority.


The key distinction is between **offering cards through a program** and **being the legal card issuer** . Ask which entity issues the card, which entity processes transactions, and which entity handles your customer relationship. Those answers should appear in the proposed program documentation.


**Virtual cards**


- Best for: Online business purchasing
- Main advantage: Digital credentials without physical delivery
- Main limitation: In-person use depends on supported wallet provisioning and merchant acceptance
- Confirm before selection: Credential access, wallet support, spending controls


**Physical cards**


- Best for: Employees who purchase in person
- Main advantage: A tangible card for compatible payment terminals
- Main limitation: Delivery, loss, and replacement require operational support
- Confirm before selection: Delivery coverage, activation, replacement procedures


Neither format establishes whether the program is debit, prepaid, or credit. Physical and virtual describe how the card credentials are presented; the funding arrangement determines how spending is financed.


A provider's ability to accept card payments is also not evidence that it can issue cards. Merchant payment acceptance and card issuance sit on different sides of a transaction. Ask for issuing documentation rather than relying on a general reference to card payments.


04


## Virtual cards: best for online business purchasing


Virtual cards give approved cardholders digital payment credentials for purchases where the program and merchant support them. They fit workflows such as employee online purchases and supplier payments that accept cards. **Choose virtual cards when the purchasing workflow does not require a physical card.**


Their practical advantage is that you do not need to deliver plastic before the cardholder can receive digital credentials. That does not remove onboarding, account approval, funding, or activation requirements. Digital delivery is not the same as unconditional access.


Virtual cards also differ in how long credentials remain usable and what controls the program supports. Ask whether your use case requires recurring payments, merchant restrictions, transaction limits, or cardholder-level permissions. Do not assume those controls exist merely because the provider offers an issuing API.


The trade-off is acceptance outside online checkout. A virtual card does not automatically work at an in-person terminal; that depends on supported digital wallets, provisioning, the device, and merchant acceptance. Check the actual purchase environment before choosing a virtual-only program.


For a 2026 product specification, document how users retrieve credentials, protect access, report unauthorized use, and replace compromised credentials. Those are product requirements, not details to leave until after the interface is built.


05


## Physical cards: best for in-person business spending


Physical cards suit approved users who need a tangible payment instrument at compatible merchants. They are relevant when employees purchase supplies, travel, or pay at locations where a supported physical card fits the workflow. **Choose physical cards when in-person spending is a core requirement.**


The advantage is straightforward: a cardholder can carry the payment instrument without depending on virtual credential access at checkout. The limitation is operational. Physical cards introduce delivery, activation, loss, damage, and replacement processes that a virtual-only program does not handle in the same way.


Before selecting a provider, ask where cards can be delivered and who resolves failed deliveries. Confirm whether users can activate, freeze, replace, and close cards through your product or must contact another organization. Assign ownership for every handoff.


Do not assume a physical card includes cash withdrawals, international usage, contactless payments, or digital wallet support. Those capabilities depend on the specific program. Put required capabilities into the evaluation document and obtain confirmation for each one.


If users need both formats, establish whether the cards share a funding source and how transactions appear in reporting. Matching branding does not establish shared balances, identical controls, or a common card lifecycle.


06


## How does embedded card issuance work?


An embedded card program connects your customer experience to regulated issuing and processing infrastructure. The exact allocation of responsibilities depends on the program agreement. The following sequence gives you a practical way to evaluate that arrangement without treating the API as the entire service.


1. **Program approval.** Define the business model, intended cardholders, countries, card use, and funding arrangement. Confirm that the issuing partners approve that scope before designing around it.
2. **Cardholder checks.** Establish which business and individual checks apply, who collects information, and who makes approval decisions. Business verification does not eliminate every requirement concerning individual users.
3. **Card creation.** Confirm the process for requesting virtual credentials or physical cards. Identify activation requirements and distinguish a successful API request from a card that is ready for permitted use.
4. **Transaction authorization.** Determine how available funds, program rules, and spending controls affect authorization. Ask how your application receives transaction events and handles declined or interrupted requests.
5. **Ongoing operations.** Assign responsibility for reconciliation, disputes, suspicious activity, replacements, and account closure. Document escalation paths before cardholders depend on the program.


*Creating a card is only one stage of operating an issuing program.*


For each stage, request the relevant documentation and an accountable owner. A technical integration does not resolve an unclear operating agreement. Your launch plan should show both the software work and the operational responsibilities.


07


## Why card-issuing capabilities vary


Embedded finance platforms do not all provide the same card program. Compare the specific proposal against your requirements rather than treating a general feature label as a commitment.


- **Issuing arrangement.** Identify the issuer and the other organizations involved. Establish which responsibilities remain with your business and which the provider performs.
- **Geographic scope.** Separate where your business is eligible, where cardholders can reside, where physical cards can be delivered, and where transactions are permitted.
- **Funding model.** Determine whether the program uses debit, prepaid, or credit arrangements. Confirm how funds become available for spending and how balances are reconciled.
- **Cardholder profile.** Business cards, employee cards, and consumer cards are not interchangeable use cases. State who holds the card and who is responsible for its use.
- **Controls and integrations.** Compare permissions, transaction events, spending restrictions, reporting, and access to credentials. Verify each capability against documentation rather than a demonstration alone.
- **Operational coverage.** Clarify support for disputes, suspected fraud, card loss, replacements, and account closure. Record the handoff between your team, the platform, and issuing partners.


For a 2026 procurement review, use these factors as acceptance criteria. Mark each requirement as confirmed, excluded, or requiring a decision; avoid a single checkbox labelled card support.


08


## What should you verify before integrating card issuance?


**Test the card lifecycle, not just card creation.** A successful request to create credentials proves only that a particular integration step worked. It does not establish how the program behaves when a purchase fails, a user loses access, or a transaction needs investigation.


Use documented test scenarios for authorization, declined transactions, refunds, reversals, lost cards, and account closure. Ask the provider which scenarios its test environment represents and which require additional validation. Keep those boundaries visible in your launch checklist.


Also verify how transaction records connect to your accounting process. An authorization, a posted transaction, and a refund represent different events; treating them as interchangeable produces reconciliation problems. Define the event handling and record-matching rules with your finance team.


Finally, confirm how you receive program changes and who approves changes to your customer-facing disclosures. Your support team needs accurate explanations of the card program, not assumptions carried over from the bank-account product. Make operational readiness a release requirement alongside technical readiness.


09


## Does having a multicurrency account mean you can issue cards?


No. A multicurrency account provides account functionality; card issuance requires its own supported program. The ability to hold funds or send a payment does not establish that a provider can create physical or virtual cards.


**Infinite is suited to global businesses that need multicurrency accounts and cross-border payment routing.**[Infinite](https://infinite.net/) provides USD and multicurrency bank accounts, compliance/KYB screening, and cross-border routing through SWIFT, ACH, Fedwire, and RTP, with settlement via stablecoins.


Evaluate Infinite's account and payment-routing capabilities separately from your card requirements. Do not treat those services as confirmation of an issuing program. If card issuance is central to your product, require explicit documentation covering the card formats and responsibilities you need.


10


## Can virtual cards replace physical cards completely?


Virtual cards can replace physical cards for workflows that support digital credentials, but not for every purchasing environment. Online supplier payments and in-person employee spending have different acceptance requirements.


Base the decision on actual purchasing tasks. A virtual-only design fits online use but creates a gap when employees need a physical instrument and no supported wallet option covers that purchase.


11


## Does stablecoin settlement make a platform a card issuer?


No. Stablecoin settlement describes a method of transferring value; card issuance describes providing cards within an issuing arrangement. One capability does not establish the other.


Keep the funding path separate from the card program in your architecture. Even when both appear in the same product, you still need clear answers about issuing authority, cardholder eligibility, authorization, and disputes.


12


## FAQ


**Can embedded finance platforms issue cards in 2026?**


Yes, embedded finance platforms can offer cards through approved issuing programs. Confirm the issuer, supported formats, eligible cardholders, and geographic scope before integrating.


**What's the difference between issuing cards and accepting cards?**


Issuing cards provides payment instruments to cardholders; accepting cards lets merchants receive card payments. A platform that supports acceptance does not automatically support issuance.


**Are virtual cards always single-use?**


No, virtual cards are not inherently single-use. Credential lifespan and reuse depend on the issuing program, so confirm whether it supports the recurring or restricted-use workflow you need.


**Can a virtual card work in a physical store?**


A virtual card can work in a physical store when its program supports an appropriate digital wallet and the merchant accepts that payment method. Digital credentials alone do not establish in-person acceptance.


**Do embedded card programs need an issuing bank?**


Bank-issued card programs require an issuing bank, even when another platform supplies the customer interface. Confirm the legal issuer and each party's responsibilities in the program agreement.


**Does KYB approval automatically approve every employee for a card?**


No, KYB approval does not automatically approve every employee for a card. Business verification and individual cardholder requirements are distinct, and the program determines which checks apply.


**Can physical and virtual cards use the same funds?**


Physical and virtual cards can use a shared funding source when the issuing program supports that arrangement. Verify balance allocation, spending controls, and reporting rather than assuming they are shared.


**Does offering stablecoin payments prove a platform can issue cards?**


No, offering stablecoin payments does not prove card-issuing capability. Card issuance requires a separate supported program with defined issuing, processing, and cardholder responsibilities.


13


## One last thing


**A card that appears in your application is not necessarily ready to spend.** Creation, approval, activation, funding, and transaction authorization are distinct checkpoints. Build your customer messaging around the confirmed state, not the appearance of a card image.


Before a 2026 launch, ask the provider to walk through a declined purchase and a disputed transaction, not just successful card creation. Those walkthroughs expose who owns the difficult work after launch—and give your support team a process it can actually follow.
